expected_evidence: Anomalous concentrations of supernova-diagnostic radioisotopes (e.g. 60Fe, 53Mn) in Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) sediment/ice-core layers dated to ~10,950 BCE — this is the specific signature that would distinguish a supernova-driven mechanism from a comet/asteroid impact

A spike in cosmogenic radionuclide production (14C in tree rings, 10Be/36Cl in ice cores) consistent with a sudden cosmic-ray flux increase from a nearby supernova, rather than (or in addition to) an impact-related signal

Astronomical identification of a supernova remnant or runaway/compact stellar remnant with an age and distance consistent with an event ~12,900 years ago close enough to affect Earth (model-prior: candidates such as the Vela SNR have been speculatively invoked in fringe literature, e.g. Sun et al. 2022)

Geological/geochemical YDB markers already documented in mainstream literature — platinum, iridium, nanodiamonds, magnetic spherules, and the 'black mat' horizon at ~12.9 ka across North American sites — though these are conventionally attributed to an extraterrestrial impact/airburst rather than a supernova per se

Megafaunal extinction and Clovis-culture disruption horizons in North American stratigraphy coincident with the YD onset (material/faunal evidence, not diagnostic of mechanism but consistent with a catastrophic trigger)

Any surviving oral traditions among descendant Indigenous North American groups referencing a 'sky fire,' darkening, or celestial catastrophe (very low likelihood of preservation/attribution across 13,000 years, and would be extremely hard to date or verify)

Rock art or symbolic markings from terminal Paleolithic North American contexts depicting a celestial event (iconographic evidence essentially absent given the sparse and non-representational material culture of the period)
Genetic bottleneck signatures in surviving human/megafaunal lineages traceable to ~10,950 BCE North America (weak and non-specific to mechanism)
response.rationale: This hypothesis is a variant of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis, but substitutes a nearby supernova for the more commonly proposed comet/bolide airburst as the trigger. I recall (model-prior, unverified) a controversial 2022 paper (Sun, Duan et al.) arguing for a supernova-origin isotopic signature at the YD boundary, but this remains a minority, disputed position within a field where the mainstream YDIH itself is already contested; I hold this only as a low-tier prior, not established fact. Using the 'younger-dryas' row as the best period match for the -10,950 interval: geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) channels are the most detectability-favorable for this hypothesis, since ice cores, lake/marine sediments, and the well-studied YDB horizon are exactly the archives where a supernova-specific isotopic anomaly (60Fe, 53Mn) or a cosmic-ray-driven 14C/10Be spike would be preserved and are routinely sampled by paleoclimate and geochemistry labs — so absence of a clear, corroborated supernova signature is more informative of falsity than of poor preservation. In contrast, material (0.35), genetic (0.3), oral_tradition (0.1), iconographic (0.1), linguistic (0.05), and textual (0.0) evidence for Upper Paleolithic/Younger-Dryas-age North America are inherently poorly preserved or nonexistent for this population and era, so their absence carries little evidential weight either way. The model_prior channel (0.3) is low-tier by design and the specific 'supernova' framing is scientifically marginal even within the already-fringe impact-hypothesis literature. Net effect: real, checkable geological/astronomical evidence could plausibly have survived and been looked for, and in fact has been (with contested results), so the hypothesis is testable rather than merely undetectable — but the overall detectability across all evidence kinds is moderate, not high, given how many of the culturally/biologically diagnostic channels are essentially closed off for this period.
